title: Why You Shouldn’t Store Potatoes and Onions Together

seo.title: Why You Shouldn’t Store Potatoes and Onions Together
seo.meta_description: Potatoes and dry onions both need cool, dry, ventilated storage, but separate containers make moisture, odors, and spoilage easier to control.
seo.search_intent: Understand why potatoes and onions are better stored separately and how to store each one.

excerpt: Potatoes and onions do not need separate bins because of one mysterious chemical reaction. Separation is useful because it improves airflow and makes it easier to keep both foods dry and remove a soft, wet, or decaying piece before it affects the small storage environment around the rest.
content_html:
A basket of potatoes and onions looks efficient: both are pantry staples and both are often kept outside the refrigerator. For longer storage, though, two ventilated containers are a better setup than one crowded basket. The reason is mostly practical—moisture, airflow, odors, and spoilage control—not a simple rule that one vegetable instantly ruins the other.

They share several storage needs

Potatoes keep best in a cool, dark, dry, well-ventilated place. Light encourages greening, while warmer conditions speed respiration and sprouting. Dry onions also need low humidity and good air movement. UC Davis lists about 65–70% relative humidity for commercial storage of cured dry onions.

You do not need a humidity meter in a home pantry to use that lesson. Closed plastic bags and damp cupboards work against both foods; mesh, slatted bins, or perforated baskets make more sense.

A bad piece creates a bad microclimate

If an onion softens and leaks moisture, or a bruised potato begins to rot, packing the two crops together holds that moisture and decaying material in a small space. Separate bins do not prevent spoilage, but they make inspection easier and reduce contact between problem pieces.

Odor is another reason. UC Davis notes that potatoes can pick up odors from volatile compounds released by other produce. Keeping strongly aromatic onions in their own basket helps preserve the relatively neutral flavor of stored potatoes.

The ethylene explanation is more complicated than social media makes it sound

You will often read that onions release ethylene and therefore make potatoes sprout. Potato physiology is not that simple. UC Davis reports that potatoes have low ethylene production and that their response depends on dose and storage conditions; low exposure can retard sprouting in some circumstances, while high concentrations can induce it. Ethylene can also encourage sprouting and decay fungi in onions.

So the useful household advice is still to separate them, but airflow, moisture, odor transfer, and inspection are better explanations than a one-line gas myth.

A pantry setup that works

  • Keep potatoes dark and ventilated.
  • Keep dry onions dry and well ventilated.
  • Do not wash either crop before storage.
  • Check the bins regularly and remove wet, soft, or rotten pieces.
  • Use separate mesh bags or baskets rather than one sealed box.

Separation is not magic. It simply gives each crop more breathing room and makes one bad onion or potato less likely to become a whole-bin problem.

faq.question: Will potatoes and onions spoil immediately if they touch?
faq.answer: No. Brief contact is not a special safety problem. Separate storage matters more when you are trying to keep them for days or weeks.

faq.question: Can I keep them in sealed plastic bags?
faq.answer: That is usually a poor choice because trapped moisture and limited airflow favor deterioration.

faq.question: Do onions always make potatoes sprout because of ethylene?
faq.answer: No. Potato responses to ethylene vary with concentration and conditions. Separate storage is better justified by ventilation, moisture, odors, and easier spoilage control.
